title: Ang 795: Bilaval begins
hookLine: Guru Nanak opens the morning raga of joy
tomorrow: can you feel joy and miss someone on the same morning?

cards: Call a CEO "team lead" and watch the face. A title that's too small can sting more than no title at all. That's how Guru Nanak opens raga Bilaval, on ang 795.
In paraphrase: you are the Sultan; if I call you chief, what kind of praise is that? Every word he has is too small for God. His answer to that problem isn't silence.

teach.h: YOU ARE THE SULTAN; I SAY CHIEF.
teach.b: Bilaval is sung as a morning raga, and Sikh tradition hears joy in it. Guru Nanak's opening hymn, in paraphrase: you are the Sultan, and I call you chief; what greatness is that?
Whatever you give me, I speak; I'm a fool, I can't find the words.
Then the refrain asks: give me understanding, so I can sing your praises and live in your will. So the joy here isn't the joy of getting it right. It's praising when the words don't fit.
And this morning raga opens a real conversation among Sikhs today.

teach.h: KEEP THE RAGA THE GURUS SET.
teach.b: Some kirtan teachers say gurbani should be sung in its own raga, the one named above each hymn, because the Gurus set the music with the words: Bilaval for a morning's joy.
Lose the raga, they say, and part of the meaning goes quiet.

teach.h: OR A TUNE EVERYONE CAN SING.
teach.b: Others say a simple, familiar tune lets more people sing along, and the shabad matters more than the scale.
A hymn nobody joins in on, they say, has also lost something. Both sides love the same hymns, and both are trying to keep them alive.
And Guru Nanak's own words sit right between them: any title is too small, so sing with what you have, and ask for understanding.

how: Each section of the Guru Granth Sahib is headed by its raga; in many gurdwaras ragis sing Bilaval's hymns in the morning, and Sikhs today debate how strictly kirtan should keep to the named raga.

where raga Suhi's last hymns are found

games.q: Bilaval's first hymn — tap the pairs.
p: what God is, in the hymn
a raga sung in the morning

s: Guru Nanak opens Bilaval saying every title for God is too small
you are the Sultan; if I call you chief, what greatness is that?
because the words fall short, Guru Nanak stops singing
he asks for understanding so he can keep singing.
all Sikhs agree kirtan must only be sung in its raga
some teachers hold to the raga; others favor familiar tunes. both love the same hymns.

games.q: your cousin calls raga kirtan 'just for old people.' you love the familiar tunes too. what is the raga side's best case?
o: the Gurus set each hymn under a raga, so the music carries part of its meaning.
older tunes simply sound holier, so they must be more correct.
familiar tunes break the rules of the Granth and shouldn't be sung.
games.why: the strongest case for the raga is the Granth's own headings: the music was set with the words. the other side's best case: a hymn nobody sings has lost something too.

practice: Listen for one sound around you right now: a bird, a fan, traffic, someone in the next room. Rest your attention on it for the sit, and let it be your morning raga, whatever time it is.
If you'd like, read Guru Nanak's opening hymn on ang 795 first.
